Companies intending to provide regulated crypto-asset services in the EU generally need authorisation from the competent authority in an EU member state.
Once authorised, a CASP can provide permitted services across other EU member states through the regulatory passporting framework.
Certain already-regulated financial institutions may provide crypto-asset services under specific notification requirements rather than obtaining a separate CASP authorisation.
MiCA establishes minimum permanent capital requirements based on the type of crypto-asset services provided, including €50,000 for Class 1, €125,000 for Class 2, and €150,000 for Class 3.
CASPs must maintain the required prudential safeguards, which are generally the higher of the applicable minimum permanent capital requirement and one-quarter of the preceding year's fixed overheads.
CASPs providing custody and administration services must protect customers' crypto-assets and funds.
Customer crypto-assets must be legally and operationally distinguished from the service provider's own assets.
CASPs must establish effective and transparent procedures for receiving and handling customer complaints.
CASPs must identify, prevent, manage and disclose conflicts of interest that could negatively affect customers.
MiCA requires CASPs to maintain appropriate governance and risk-management arrangements.
MiCA establishes rules against market abuse involving crypto-assets admitted to trading or for which admission to trading has been requested.
MiCA's stablecoin-related provisions concerning asset-referenced tokens and e-money tokens began applying on 30 June 2024.
Most other provisions, including the main CASP authorisation and conduct requirements, began applying on 30 December 2024.

The EU's Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA), Regulation (EU) 2023/1114, requires crypto-asset service providers (CASPs) to be authorized before providing crypto-asset services in the EU.
MiCA subjects crypto-asset service providers (CASPs) to authorization, prudential, governance, client-asset, complaints, and conflict-of-interest rules in the EU.

A person may not provide crypto-asset services in the EU unless authorized as a CASP by the relevant national competent authority, or unless it qualifies as an already-authorized credit institution, investment firm, e-money institution, or similar entity under specified conditions.
A crypto-asset service provider (CASP) must be a legal person with a registered office in an EU member state where it provides at least part of its services.
At least one director of a crypto-asset service provider (CASP) must reside in the EU and have effective management there.

Crypto-asset service providers (CASPs) must maintain safeguards at least equal to the higher of the applicable permanent minimum capital requirement in MiCA Annex IV or one-quarter of the preceding year's fixed overheads.
The management of crypto-asset service providers (CASPs) must be fit and proper, with adequate knowledge, experience, skills, and time.
Crypto-asset service providers (CASPs) must maintain policies to prevent money laundering, terrorist financing, and other financial crime.
Crypto-asset service providers (CASPs) must keep clients' crypto-assets and funds separate from the firm's own assets.
Crypto-asset service providers (CASPs) must not use clients' crypto-assets and funds for the firm's own account.
Crypto-asset service providers (CASPs) must operate prompt, fair, and transparent complaint procedures.
Crypto-asset service providers (CASPs) must identify, prevent, manage, and disclose conflicts of interest.
Crypto-asset service providers (CASPs) must act honestly, fairly, and professionally in clients' best interests.
MiCA entered into force on 29 June 2023.

MiCA's CASP provisions apply from 30 December 2024, with transitional arrangements allowing certain pre-existing nationally authorized providers to continue until 1 July 2026 or until their MiCA authorization is granted or refused.
